content: The shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) is a treatment protocol lasting 9–12 months, utilizing only oral medications. This regimen is recommended for eligible patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB who have not been exposed to second-line TB drugs included in this regimen for more than one month and who do not have fluoroquinolone resistance. This recommendation is conditional, with very low certainty in the evidence. In 2019, programmatic data from South Africa, where this regimen was implemented routinely, led the World Health Organization (WHO) to revise its recommendations on standardized shorter regimens. An analysis of 10,152 patient records from South Africa (January–June 2017) compared the effectiveness of the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen to a standardized injectable-containing shorter regimen. Based on this analysis, WHO reaffirmed its conditional recommendation for the shorter all-oral regimen as a treatment option for eligible MDR/RR-TB patients. The implementation of this regimen is expected to improve the management of drug-resistant TB within TB programs. However, the treatment still requires the use of seven agents, some of which have significant toxicity, for up to 12 months. Patients will need support to manage the challenges of TB treatment, including daily adherence, adverse drug reactions, indirect costs, and stigma. Eligibility for this regimen is critical, as its widespread use could benefit both patients and health systems. However, careful patient selection is necessary. In South Africa, eligible patients under programmatic conditions showed better efficacy with this regimen compared to previously recommended longer regimens without new drugs or injectable-containing shorter regimens. There was also a lower likelihood of loss to follow-up. No data were available for comparison with longer all-oral regimens recommended by WHO in 2018. When deciding on the use of this regimen, several eligibility criteria must be considered, including patient and clinician preferences. If the shorter regimen cannot be used, the patient should be reassessed for a longer all-oral regimen. In some cases, clinicians may opt for a longer regimen even for eligible patients due to uncertainty about drug susceptibility, especially when immediate treatment initiation is required before drug susceptibility testing (DST) results are available. The extent of TB disease is an important factor in determining regimen options, alongside DST and other considerations. Extensive TB disease is defined as bilateral cavitary disease or extensive parenchymal damage on chest radiography. In children under 15 years, advanced disease is usually defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on chest radiography. Severe extrapulmonary TB is defined as miliary TB or TB meningitis. In children, extrapulmonary forms of disease other than lymphadenopathy (e.g., peripheral nodes or isolated mediastinal mass without compression) are considered severe. Chest radiography is emphasized as a key diagnostic tool alongside patient-clinician interaction. Testing for fluoroquinolone susceptibility is recommended before starting the shorter all-oral regimen to exclude resistance. Isoniazid remains a key component of shorter regimens, even in the presence of low-level resistance, when used at higher doses as part of combination therapy. Mutations in the inhA promoter or katG regions confer resistance to isoniazid, with low-level resistance associated with inhA mutations and high-level resistance with katG mutations. Mutations in the inhA promoter are also linked to resistance to ethionamide and prothionamide. The presence of both inhA and katG mutations suggests that high-dose isoniazid and thioamides are ineffective, making the shorter regimen unsuitable. In the absence of individual mutation data, knowledge of mutation patterns from drug-resistance surveillance in the relevant epidemiological setting may guide decisions. Rapid methods to detect resistance to clofazimine and bedaquiline are not yet available, but phenotypic DST can be performed using established critical concentrations. Ideally, phenotypic DST should be conducted at treatment initiation or with the first strain isolated. The shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen recommended by WHO in 2020 includes bedaquiline, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, ethionamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, and pyrazinamide for 4 months (extendable to 6 months if sputum smear or culture remains positive at the end of the fourth month), followed by 5 months of levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Bedaquiline is used for 6 months. The regimen is standardized and should not be modified in terms of composition or duration, except in specific cases such as extending the initial phase if sputum smear or culture does not convert by the fourth month (but not beyond 6 months in total). Prothionamide may replace ethionamide, and moxifloxacin may replace levofloxacin. Other changes, such as removing ethionamide in the presence of inhA mutations or replacing ethionamide or clofazimine with linezolid, have not been studied and are not recommended in programmatic use. If a patient started on the shorter regimen is later found to be ineligible due to undetected resistance or the emergence of additional resistance, further resistance may have developed. Repeated DST is necessary to guide the composition of a longer regimen. Conversely, patients on a longer regimen who are later found eligible for the shorter regimen can be switched, provided treatment has not exceeded one month. However, there is limited experience with such changes. If switched, the shorter regimen should be given for its full duration without changes to its composition or duration. The shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen can be used in people living with HIV (PLHIV), including those on antiretroviral therapy (ART). However, overlapping toxicities and drug-drug interactions between TB drugs (e.g., moxifloxacin, clofazimine, bedaquiline) and antiretrovirals (e.g., efavirenz, ritonavir) must be considered. Ritonavir may increase bedaquiline exposure, potentially raising the risk of adverse reactions. Therefore, the combination of bedaquiline with ritonavir should be avoided or used with caution. Data from South Africa showed that most PLHIV receiving this regimen were also on ART (95%). Close monitoring is advised, as data in this subgroup remain limited. ART should be initiated early, and PLHIV on this regimen will require prophylactic medication for opportunistic infections, adherence support, and close monitoring of immune status biomarkers. The regimen may also be used in children aged 6 years and above, although data for this age group are sparse. The medicines in the regimen, except for bedaquiline, have been part of MDR-TB regimens for many years in both adults and children. Adverse drug reactions are well-documented, and drug dosages are established. Dispersible and palatable formulations should be used when possible. Bedaquiline tablets suspended in water have equivalent bioavailability to whole tablets and can be used in children until child-friendly formulations become available. For pregnant and lactating women, the regimen contains ethionamide, which is usually contraindicated in pregnancy due to adverse effects on the fetus observed in animal studies and the lack of adequate human studies. Until better safety profiles are established, individualized longer regimens can be designed to avoid known toxicities. Patients with rifampicin-resistant TB without MDR-TB may be treated with the shorter all-oral regimen if isoniazid resistance is not confirmed. For patients with extensive disease, preference should be given to longer all-oral regimens, as programmatic data on the shorter regimen did not include such patients. Therefore, recommendations for the shorter regimen cannot be extrapolated to this subgroup. Adjustments may be required depending on the specific disease location, as some drugs (e.g., ethambutol) do not penetrate the cerebrospinal fluid well.
